readingInstruction: Read Psalm 89:38-52. Last unit you read the first half of this psalm, which celebrates God’s covenant with David. Today comes the second half, which seems to contradict it. Read it as the prayer of someone living the fall of Jerusalem.
settingTheScene: Psalm 89 changes in verse 38. After thirty-seven verses of praise for God’s oath to David, the psalmist turns and says, “But now you have cast off and rejected.” The king is humiliated, the crown is in the dust, the walls are broken. This is the psalm that fits the end of 2 Kings: the line of David has fallen, and the promise seems to have failed.
observation: “But now you have cast off and rejected; you are full of wrath against your anointed” (v. 38).
“You have renounced the covenant with your servant; you have defiled his crown in the dust” (v. 39).
“You have breached all his walls; you have laid his strongholds in ruins” (v. 40).
“You have not made him stand in battle” (v. 43).
“You have cut short the days of his youth; you have covered him with shame” (v. 45).
“How long, O LORD? Will you hide yourself forever? How long will your wrath burn like fire?” (v. 46).
“Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David?” (v. 49).
“Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and Amen” (v. 52).
interpretation:
The contrast between the two halves is deliberate and honest. The first half quotes God’s oath: “I will not violate my covenant.” The second half describes what it looks like to live as though God had violated it. The psalmist does not pretend that the promise and the experience match. He says, “You have renounced the covenant.” It is the language of a person who is not hiding his confusion.

Yet he does not walk away. Every complaint is addressed to God. That is the mark of faith in this psalm: the very God who seems to have broken his word is the one the psalmist keeps speaking to. “Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David?” He holds God to his own promise.

The ending is one of the most surprising in the Psalter. After forty verses of lament, the psalm closes with praise: “Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and Amen.” This is a doxology that marks the end of Book 3. Nothing has been resolved. The question is still open. But the psalmist blesses God anyway. Sometimes faith is the choice to bless when you cannot see how the story will end.

For Israel, the answer was long in coming. The line of David looked dead for six hundred years. But the answer came in Bethlehem, in a son of David who would never be removed.
connection: Acts 13:32-34 says that God fulfilled the promise to David by raising Jesus from the dead. Luke 1:32-33 announces that the Lord will give him the throne of his father David. Romans 1:3-4 says Jesus was descended from David according to the flesh and declared Son of God by the resurrection. Revelation 5:5 says the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered. Romans 15:13 prays for hope in the God of hope.
application:
When your experience does not match God’s promise, pray as the psalmist did: honestly, and to God.

Choose to bless the LORD even in an unanswered season. Say “Blessed be the LORD forever” aloud.

Thank God for Jesus, the answer to the question of Psalm 89.
prayerPrompts: Ask God where his steadfast love is, in your own honest words.
Bring him your questions because you have nowhere else to go.
Bless him even in the hard questions.
